sentences.text:
Sasanka Sekhar Das vs The State Of West Bengal & Ors on 4
February, 2026
 In The High Court At Calcutta
 Constitutional Writ Jurisdiction
Appellate Side

Present:
The Hon'ble Justice Madhuresh Prasad
 And
The Hon'ble Justice Prasenjit Biswas
 M.A.T. 1471 of 2019
 Sasanka Sekhar Das
 Vs.
 The State of West Bengal & Ors.

For the Appellant : Mr. S. P. Dalapati,
 Mr. Asamdipta Santra

For the Municipal Corporation : Mr. Ramchandra Guchhait
Heard on : 04.02.2026
Judgment on : 04.02.2026

MADHURESH PRASAD, J.:
1. Heard learned advocate for the writ petitioner and the learned advocate for the respondents.
2. The petitioner/appellant filed a writ petition wherein he stated that he purchased some land from one Kanan Behari Nanda and others on 20.09.1971 vide deed no. 2913.

He thereafter stated that on 24.02.2012 he made a representation to the Sub Divisional Officer, Irrigation Kuemari Sub-division ,Haidighi, South 24 Parganas seeking an award and compensation for the lands stating that the respondent authorities without initiating any acquisition proceeding are going to construct some embankment on the lands which lie on the bank of the river.
By stating that the respondent authorities took no action on the petitioner's representation dated 24.02.2012, the writ petition was filed by the petitioner in 2014.

The same was dismissed by the Hon'ble Single Judge with cost of Rs.
2,000/-.

sentences.text: The learned advocate for the appellant submits that without initiating any acquisition proceeding the State authorities cannot take possession or acquire any land of a citizen.
The submission is that the authorities have utilized the petitioner's lands lying on the river bank for erecting an embankment thereupon for a public purpose.
In view of such utilization for a public purpose, even if land was given with consent of the petitioner, the State is under a bounden duty to pay compensation.

He has relied upon decisions of the Apex Court in the case of Karnataka Electricity Board -Vs.- State of Karnataka And Others reported in (2002) 3 SCC 141 (paragraph 8 & 9), Radhy Shyam (Dead) through Lrs. And Others -Vs.- State of Uttar Pradesh And Others

entities.text: Karnataka Electricity Board -Vs.- State of Karnataka And Others reported in (2002) 3 SCC 141 (paragraph 8 & 9)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: reported in (2011) 5 SCC 553 (Paragraph 77).
It is submitted that as per the Constitutional mandate in Article 300A, the law protects a person from forcible dispossession.
Even in exercise of eminent domain a person's property, if acquired or taken over, the same casts an obligation on the State to pay compensation which has not been done in the present case.
4. Relying on another decision of the Apex Court in the case of Amrit Lal Berry -Vs.- Collector of Central Excise, New Delhi & Ors. reported in (1975) 4 SCC 714.

entities.text: Amrit Lal Berry -Vs.- Collector of Central Excise, New Delhi & Ors. reported in (1975) 4 SCC 714
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is submitted that in view of the nature of violation of the petitioner's rights, the Writ Court exercising jurisdiction under Article 226 should pass appropriate orders directing the authorities to acquire the petitioner's land in accordance with law and pay compensation to the petitioner.
5. The learned advocate for the State has made two fold submissions.
The first is that in the writ petition, the writ petitioner did not disclose any details of the land which the petitioner alleges to have been utilized for a public purpose.
6. The second submission is referring to the deed dated 20.09.1971.
He submits that a copy of the same has been annexed in the writ petition wherein the details of land conveyed through the deed has been shown as bearing Dag No. 431.

The details of land in the deed is at variance with the details of land stated by the petitioner in his representation dated 24.02.2012, made before the Sub Divisional Officer, seeking compensation for the lands in question.
7. Therefore, from the averments made in the writ petition no case is made out with reference to any fixed details/ documents supporting the petitioner's claim to the lands.
Such vague and sketchy claim by way of a writ petition with respect to right, title and possession of land, therefore, should not be looked into by this Court.
8. It is further submitted that the authorities filed an affidavit-in-opposition in the writ proceeding.

It was the specific stand of the authorities that in view of the flow of the river in the delta region there is frequent change in the alignment and the expanse of land on account of the forces of weathering due to river water flowing from the lands to the sea, or the sea waves hitting and eroding the land mass.
In 2001-2002 a situation arose where saline water was entering the fields and property of the local people who reside near the delta.

2 9.

entities.text: Sasanka Sekhar Das vs The State Of West Bengal & Ors
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is under such circumstances that the local people for safeguarding their interest voluntarily and without any land compensation requested the authorities to take appropriate steps for ensuring that the "ring bundh" a kind of temporary structure was created and maintained for preventing ingress of saline water into the country side.
The averments in the affidavit- in-opposition filed by the State were not responded to by the writ petitioner.
10. We have considered the rival submissions, and gone through records.
We find force in submission of the learned advocate for the State that the writ petition does not disclose any details of land claimed by the writ petitioner.

The submission that there is a variation between the details of land in the deed dated 20.09.1971, and representation submitted by the petitioner on 24.02.2012 is also reflected from the records, though the petitioner's learned advocate has tried to explain the variation by saying that Plot/Dag numbers have changed on account of a survey intervening between the sale deed; and submission of the representation.

11. We also find force in the submission of the learned advocate for the State that the State specifically took a stand as noted above which remains undisputed by the writ petitioner, as no reply was filed thereto inviting the consequence of non traverse.

12. Insofar as the other submissions that in exercise of eminent domain, even if with consent of a land owner, lands are taken, then obligation is cast on the State to pay compensation, we find that the plea raised by the learned advocate is not supported by the decision relied upon.

In so far as the Apex Court decision Karnataka Electricity Board (supra) is concerned, we find that the decision therein is on a factual foundation that the lands had been given by the landowner by an agreement for establishing electricity power station.
However, in the agreement itself there was a clause that a particular amount of compensation would be payable to the person giving the land (land owner).

No document whatsoever has been brought to the notice of the Court in the present case, from which it can be inferred that any land of the writ petitioner was utilized by the respondent/s.
13.
Insofar as the Apex Court decision Radhy Shyam (supra) is concerned, we are of the considered opinion that the same also does not inure to the petitioner's benefits.
Paragraph 77 of the judgment relied upon does not support the case of the petitioner.
The paragraph relied upon is an exposition of principles underlying the exercising of eminent domain to acquire a property.
In the present case such factual foundation regarding utilization or acquisition of petitioner's land is missing.

We also consider it worth taking note of a fact that though utilization of land of the local people for irrigating ring bundh was done in the year 2001-2002, the writ petitioner raised a claim that his lands was also acquired by making a representation dated 24.02.2012 before the sub-Divisional Officer,
Irrigation, Kuemari (I) Sub-Division, Raidighi, South 24 Parganas.
The issue thus has been raised by the writ petitioner after more than a decade from the time when as per State's case land of the local people was offered voluntarily and utilized.
14. In the present case, the petitioner claims that his land was utilized, but without any details of land said to be acquired, or any document to support such contention.
The State in the affidavit has not admitted to such utilization and the same remains a disputed issue of fact.

Such a claim nay be pursued in appropriate civil proceedings, and this Court does not propose to go into such disputed Sasanka Sekhar Das vs The State Of West Bengal & Ors on 4 February, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/130319378/
3 issues of fact, when even details of land were not stated by the petitioner in his writ petition.

sentences.text: We consider it appropriate to refer to and rely upon a recent decision of the Apex Court in the case of State of Uttar Pradesh and Another vs. Ehsan and Another reported in (2024) 14 SCC 269 wherein the conclusion of the Apex Court with regard to similar claim of the writ petitioner was being considered.

entities.text: State of Uttar Pradesh and Another vs. Ehsan and Another reported in (2024) 14 SCC 269
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
In paragraph 35 the Apex Court concluded:
"35.

(d) that in the earlier two rounds of litigation, the High Court refrained from deciding the issue of possession of the surplus land even though that issue had arisen directly between the parties; and (e) that infraction of the prescribed statutory procedure for taking possession cannot be the sole basis to discard the State's claim of possession, when it is stated to have been taken long before the date the issue is raised, we are of the considered view that the High Court should have refrained from deciding the issue with regard to taking of actual possession of the surplus land prior to the cut-off date specified in the Repeal Act, 1999.

Instead, the writ petitioner should have been relegated to a suit."
15.
We, therefore, find no infirmity in the decision of the Hon'ble Single Judge rejecting the writ petition, which takes us to the issue of cost of Rs. 2,000/- imposed by the Hon'ble Single Judge.
Having considered the petitioner's case on merits, we are not inclined to sustain the cost.

16. Before parting with the judgment we make it clear that the present order may not be deemed to be an expression on the petitioner's claim to title with respect to any land and we leave such issues open to be agitated in an appropriate civil proceeding relying upon evidence and witnesses, in accordance with law.

17. The appeal is dismissed.
